# Applied Statistics for Data Science, Machine Learning, and AI Engineers

> A free, open-source, interactive statistics handbook for data scientists, ML engineers,
> and AI engineers. Covers descriptive and robust statistics, hypothesis testing, probability
> distributions, regression (including multiple regression, categorical encoding, and
> regularization), cross-validation, regression splines and LOESS/GAMs, decision trees, random
> forests, gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM), and Bayesian methods (conjugate models,
> robust and hierarchical regression, PyMC, model comparison and Bayes factors, Gaussian
> processes including classification, BART, Bayesian gradient boosting with quantile
> regression and conformal prediction, and Bayesian A/B testing with latent-subgroup
> heterogeneity) in Python. Every one of the book's 125+ figures is a live, draggable Plotly
> chart with no server or setup required, and every figure has a matching, runnable Python
> script.

Live book: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/
Source repository: https://github.com/RudrenduPaul/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers
License: CC BY 4.0 (book text), MIT (plotting code)
Format: 15 chapters, 3 parts, plain Markdown source, one running dataset (simulated checkout-API response times) followed end to end

## Frequently asked questions

**Is this book free?** Yes. The full text is free to read online at the live book link above, with no paywall, signup, or account required.

**Can I reuse the text or figures?** Yes, under CC BY 4.0 (text) and MIT (code), with attribution to Rudrendu Paul.

**Does reading this book require a Jupyter kernel or a running Python server?** No. Every figure is pre-rendered to a self-contained interactive HTML page, so the live book works from a static file server and needs nothing more than a browser.

**Does this book cover statistical significance, p-values, and alpha?** Yes. Chapter 2 (Hypothesis Testing) covers the p-value, the significance threshold (alpha), and explicitly warns against the p-value-as-probability-of-truth misreading. Chapter 4 (Regression Modeling) separately covers statistical vs. practical significance, showing how a fixed-size effect can cross the significance threshold purely because sample size grew.

**Does this book cover Type I and Type II errors and statistical power?** Yes. Chapter 2 covers Type I error (false positive), Type II error (false negative), the trade-off between them as the significance threshold moves, and statistical power (1 minus beta) as a function of sample size and effect size, each with an interactive figure.

**Does this book cover precision, recall, F1, and ROC/AUC?** Yes. Chapter 7 (Tree-Based Methods) has a dedicated section on evaluating a classifier, with an interactive confusion-matrix figure where dragging the classification threshold live-updates precision, recall, F1, and the ROC curve in the same view.

**What is the difference between a p-value and the probability the null hypothesis is true?** A p-value is computed by assuming the null hypothesis is true, and it measures how surprising the observed data would be under that assumption. Per the American Statistical Association, a p-value "does not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true." Chapter 2 covers this distinction directly.

**What is the difference between a confidence interval and a Bayesian credible interval?** A confidence interval is a statement about a repeated procedure: 95% of intervals generated across repeated experiments would contain the true value, with no probability claim about any single interval. A credible interval is a direct probability statement about the parameter given the observed data: a 95% credible interval means a 95% posterior probability the parameter lies in that range. Chapter 9 covers both side by side on the same dataset.

**How does Ridge regression relate to a Gaussian prior?** Ridge regression's L2 penalty is mathematically equivalent to placing a Gaussian prior on the regression coefficients and taking the posterior mode; Lasso's L1 penalty corresponds to a Laplace prior. Chapter 4's Bayesian preview and Chapter 9's full treatment both derive this, and the interactive figure shows the posterior narrowing and sliding toward zero as the prior variance shrinks, mirroring what Ridge's penalty term does algebraically.

**How does Bayesian A/B testing differ from a classical significance test?** Chapter 14 covers this end to end: Bayesian A/B testing produces a posterior distribution over each variant's conversion rate, a win probability, and an expected-loss stopping rule, instead of a single p-value. It does not fully solve the peeking problem: undisciplined repeated checks still bias the result, but a Bayesian posterior does not inflate mechanically the way a repeated frequentist significance test does.

**What is the difference between WAIC/PSIS-LOO and k-fold cross-validation?** They answer the same generalization question, how well does this model predict new data, but PSIS-LOO and WAIC (Chapter 10) compute it directly from a Bayesian model's posterior draws, while k-fold cross-validation (Chapter 5) refits the model on held-out folds. PSIS-LOO is worth its setup cost when the model is Bayesian anyway or the dataset is too small for stable refitting; k-fold CV remains faster for routine comparisons.

**Why does a random forest split on only a random subset of predictors at each split?** Restricting each split to a random subset of predictors (Chapter 7, typically m ≈ √p for classification) forces trees to occasionally split on weaker predictors instead of always defaulting to the strongest one, which decorrelates the trees so averaging reduces variance more effectively.

**Why are boosted trees kept shallow while random forest trees are grown deep?** A random forest (Chapter 7) controls variance by averaging many deep, individually overfit trees. A boosted model (Chapter 8) keeps its trees shallow on purpose, often 2 to 6 levels, so no single tree overcorrects, leaving the learning rate and tree count to control the ensemble's overall complexity instead.

**Why does the mean sometimes disagree badly with the median even in a large dataset?** The mean is sensitive to every value including extreme outliers, while the median only depends on which value sits in the middle of the sorted data. Chapter 1 covers this alongside robust alternatives, the trimmed mean, the median absolute deviation (MAD), and the interquartile range (IQR), each built to resist the same handful of outliers that can drag the mean and variance far from what most of the data looks like.

**When should Spearman correlation be used instead of Pearson correlation?** Pearson correlation only detects linear relationships; Spearman correlation (Chapter 1) measures whether two variables move together monotonically, even if the relationship curves, by correlating their ranks instead of their raw values. A relationship can have a strong Spearman correlation and a much weaker Pearson correlation if it is monotonic but not a straight line.

**How does robust regression handle outliers differently than ordinary least squares?** Ordinary least squares minimizes squared error, so a single extreme point can pull the fitted line far from the bulk of the data because its error gets squared. Chapter 9 covers robust Bayesian regression with a Student-t likelihood in place of a Normal likelihood: the Student-t distribution's heavier tails mean an extreme point is treated as a plausible-but-rare draw rather than evidence the line must bend toward it, so the fit stays closer to the majority of the data.

**What is a hierarchical (multilevel) Bayesian model and when does it help?** A hierarchical model (Chapter 9 and Chapter 14) fits a per-group estimate for each group in the data while letting every group borrow statistical strength from the others, through a shared population-level distribution. It matters most for groups with little data of their own: a group with only a handful of observations shrinks toward the population's typical behavior instead of reporting a noisy, overconfident estimate built from almost nothing.

**What does it mean when a Bayesian model's sampler reports a "divergence"?** A divergence (Chapter 9) is Hamiltonian Monte Carlo's own warning that it could not accurately explore some region of the posterior, most often triggered by a funnel-shaped geometry common in hierarchical models where a group-level variance parameter and its associated per-group offsets are tightly coupled. A non-centered parameterization, which separates the offset from the variance in how the model is written, resolves the funnel and removes the divergences without changing what the model represents.

**Can a Gaussian process be used for classification, not just regression?** Yes. Chapter 11 covers Gaussian process classification: a latent function is passed through a sigmoid link into a Bernoulli likelihood, letting the GP's flexible, non-parametric prior over functions produce a non-monotonic decision boundary that a plain logistic regression's straight-line boundary cannot represent.

**What is the difference between WAIC/PSIS-LOO and a Bayes factor?** WAIC and PSIS-LOO (Chapter 10) estimate how well a model predicts new data, computed directly from the posterior draws a model run produces, with no need to refit anything. A Bayes factor instead compares the total marginal likelihood of two models across their entire prior, which makes it far more sensitive to the prior chosen and to sample size; Chapter 10 covers why this book leads with WAIC/PSIS-LOO for routine model comparison and treats Bayes factors as a narrower, prior-sensitive tool.

**What is quantile regression and why not just predict the mean?** Quantile regression (Chapter 13) predicts a specific quantile of the outcome's distribution, such as the 95th percentile, instead of its mean. This matters whenever the tail of a distribution is the part that causes a problem: a mean-latency model can look safely under an SLA while the measured P95 latency has breached it, a gap only a quantile model would have caught.

**What is conformal prediction and how does it differ from a Bayesian credible interval?** Conformal prediction (Chapter 13) builds a prediction interval with a distribution-free coverage guarantee calibrated directly from held-out data, without assuming any particular likelihood or prior. A Bayesian credible interval (Chapter 9, Chapter 12) instead depends on the model's assumed likelihood and prior being reasonably correct; conformal prediction trades that model-dependence for a guarantee that holds regardless of whether the underlying model is well specified.

**Can an A/B test look like a clear win on average while still harming a subgroup of users?** Yes. Chapter 14 covers this directly with a latent (unobserved) subgroup heterogeneity example: a checkout redesign that looks like a clear win in the aggregate can still be harming a subgroup, such as first-time buyers, whose identity was never logged as a segment column, something a two-component mixture model can surface that a single pooled analysis cannot.

**What is a sample ratio mismatch (SRM) and why does it matter for A/B testing?** A sample ratio mismatch (Chapter 14) is a gap between an A/B test's intended traffic split and its observed split, checked with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test. An undetected SRM, often caused by a bug like a redirect that drops some of one variant's traffic without any visible error, invalidates the whole test's conclusion regardless of how the conversion-rate comparison itself came out.

## Key definitions

- **p-value**: the probability of observing data at least as extreme as what was measured, computed under the assumption the null hypothesis is true. Covered in Chapter 2.
- **Statistical significance / alpha**: a pre-chosen significance threshold (commonly 0.05); a result is "statistically significant" when its p-value falls below alpha. Covered in Chapter 2 and Chapter 4.
- **Type I error**: rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive). Covered in Chapter 2.
- **Type II error**: failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative). Covered in Chapter 2.
- **Statistical power**: the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis, equal to 1 minus the Type II error rate. Covered in Chapter 2.
- **Cohen's d / effect size**: a standardized measure of the size of a difference between two groups, independent of sample size, distinct from a p-value's significance verdict. Covered in Chapter 2.
- **Precision**: of the cases predicted positive, the share that are true positives. Covered in Chapter 7.
- **Recall**: of the cases that are positive, the share correctly predicted positive. Covered in Chapter 7.
- **F1 score**: the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Covered in Chapter 7.
- **ROC curve / AUC**: the ROC curve plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate across every classification threshold; AUC is the area under that curve. Covered in Chapter 7.
- **Confidence interval**: a range constructed so that, across repeated experiments, a stated percentage of such intervals would contain the true parameter value. Covered in Chapter 4 and contrasted with credible intervals in Chapter 9.
- **Credible interval**: a Bayesian posterior range with a direct probability interpretation, a 95% credible interval means a 95% posterior probability the parameter lies in that range. Covered in Chapter 9.
- **Ridge regression**: linear regression with an L2 penalty on coefficient size, equivalent to a Gaussian prior in the Bayesian view. Covered in Chapter 4 and Chapter 9.
- **Lasso regression**: linear regression with an L1 penalty that can shrink coefficients all the way to zero, equivalent to a Laplace prior in the Bayesian view. Covered in Chapter 4 and Chapter 9.
- **Variance inflation factor (VIF)**: a diagnostic for multicollinearity among regression predictors, measuring how much a coefficient's variance inflates because that predictor is correlated with the others. Covered in Chapter 4.
- **Simpson's paradox**: a trend that appears in several groups of data reverses or disappears when the groups are combined, driven by a confounding variable. Covered in Chapter 1, referenced again in Chapter 15.
- **PSIS-LOO**: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation, a Bayesian model-comparison metric computed from posterior draws without refitting the model. Covered in Chapter 5 and Chapter 10.
- **Gaussian process**: a Bayesian, non-parametric regression method that returns a full posterior distribution over possible curves rather than a single fitted line. Covered in Chapter 6 and Chapter 11.
- **BART (Bayesian Additive Regression Trees)**: a sum-of-weak-trees ensemble fit by MCMC that returns a full posterior over predictions instead of a single point estimate. Covered in Chapter 7 and Chapter 12.
- **Win probability / expected loss**: Bayesian A/B testing decision metrics: the posterior probability one variant beats another, and the expected cost of choosing wrong given current uncertainty. Covered in Chapter 14.
- **Hypergeometric distribution**: the distribution of the count of successes drawn without replacement from a finite population, distinct from the binomial distribution's with-replacement assumption. Covered in Chapter 3.
- **Robust (Student-t) regression**: a Bayesian regression variant that replaces the Normal likelihood with a Student-t likelihood, so its heavier tails keep outliers from dominating the fit the way ordinary least squares' squared error does. Covered in Chapter 9.
- **Hierarchical (multilevel) model**: a model that fits a per-group estimate for every group while letting each group borrow statistical strength from a shared population-level distribution, shrinking sparsely observed groups toward the population's typical behavior. Covered in Chapter 9 and Chapter 14.
- **MCMC divergence**: a warning from a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler that it failed to explore some region of the posterior with good accuracy, often caused by a funnel-shaped geometry in hierarchical models and fixed with a non-centered parameterization. Covered in Chapter 9.
- **Bayesian model averaging**: blending several models' posterior predictive distributions using their relative predictive weights, instead of selecting a single best model. Covered in Chapter 10.
- **Bayes factor**: a ratio of two models' marginal likelihoods, more prior-sensitive and sample-size-sensitive than predictive-accuracy metrics like WAIC or PSIS-LOO. Covered in Chapter 10.
- **Gaussian process classification**: a Gaussian process whose latent function passes through a sigmoid or probit link into a Bernoulli likelihood, producing a flexible, non-parametric decision boundary. Covered in Chapter 11.
- **Quantile regression**: predicting a specific quantile of an outcome's distribution, such as the 95th percentile, rather than its mean, to catch tail behavior a mean-based model would miss. Covered in Chapter 13.
- **Conformal prediction**: a distribution-free method for building a prediction interval with a coverage guarantee calibrated from held-out data, independent of any assumed likelihood. Covered in Chapter 13.
- **Sample ratio mismatch (SRM)**: a gap between an A/B test's intended and observed traffic split, checked with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test; an undetected SRM invalidates the test's conclusion. Covered in Chapter 14.
- **Latent subgroup heterogeneity**: when an experiment's effect varies by an unobserved factor not logged as a segment column, detectable with a mixture model even though no segment label exists to condition on directly. Covered in Chapter 14.

## Part 1: Foundations of Applied Statistics

### Chapter 1: Introduction to Descriptive Statistics
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-01-descriptive-statistics.html

Using a simulated checkout-API latency dataset, this chapter shows how measures of center, spread, and co-movement can each mislead a reader when picked or applied carelessly, then covers robust alternatives (trimmed mean, IQR, MAD) and Spearman correlation for monotonic-but-nonlinear relationships, closing with Simpson's paradox as a warning about confounding. Two historical case studies anchor the chapter: the 1936 Literary Digest election poll (a 10-million-person sample that still missed the outcome by 24 points) and Charig et al.'s 1986 kidney-stone treatment study.

- Key concepts: mean/median/mode; variance and standard deviation vs. percentile thresholds; robust statistics (trimmed mean, IQR, median absolute deviation, Tukey's fence, modified z-score); covariance and Pearson correlation vs. Spearman rank correlation; selection bias (sampling, self-selection, nonresponse, recall); mean imputation; Simpson's paradox and confounding variables
- Interactive figures: fig-mean-median (mean vs. median as slow-request contamination rises), fig-std-percentile (a mean-plus-k-SD threshold vs. fixed percentile lines), fig-cov-corr (correlation strength from 0 to 0.85), fig-metric-correlations (a grayscale-safe correlation-ellipse matrix across five cluster health metrics under three traffic regimes), fig-skew-kurt (a distribution morphing from symmetric to right-skewed), fig-literary-digest (the 1936 poll's prediction vs. the election outcome), fig-mean-imputation (imputation narrowing spread as missing data grows), fig-simpsons (the kidney-stone reversal by pooling)
- FAQ: Why do on-call dashboards trust median and percentile latency over mean latency? The mean is pulled by every value including extremes, so a small share of slow requests drags it well above the median while percentile lines stay fixed at whatever share of traffic they were defined to capture. This is why the Google SRE book recommends defining SLIs on percentiles rather than the mean.

### Chapter 2: Hypothesis Testing
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-02-hypothesis-testing.html

Using a caching-layer rollout as its running example, this chapter builds the full hypothesis-testing toolkit from single-mean tests through ANOVA, chi-squared, ANCOVA, experimental design, and non-parametric alternatives, adds confidence intervals for a mean and a proportion, the two-proportion z-test, the multiple-comparisons problem, and the sequential-testing/peeking problem, and repeatedly stresses what a p-value does and does not mean.

- Key concepts: Z-test and t-test; p-value interpretation; Type I/Type II errors and statistical power; Cohen's d and effect size; confidence intervals for a mean and a proportion; the two-proportion z-test; the multiple-comparisons problem; sequential testing and the peeking/optional-stopping problem; paired vs. Welch's unpaired t-test; ANOVA/ANCOVA and chi-squared tests; Wilcoxon rank-sum and Kruskal-Wallis non-parametric tests
- Interactive figures: fig-t-vs-normal (t-distribution tails vs. degrees of freedom), fig-error-tradeoff (Type I vs. Type II error as the threshold moves), fig-power-curve (power rising with sample size), fig-ci-bootstrap (a bootstrapped confidence interval for a mean), fig-peeking (false-positive rate inflating under repeated early stopping), fig-permutation-null (a permutation test's null distribution against the observed statistic), fig-anova-between-within (F and p as between-group gap widens), fig-nonparametric (t-test vs. Wilcoxon rank-sum stability under outliers)
- FAQ: Does a p-value of 0.03 mean there's a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true? No. A p-value assumes the null hypothesis is true and measures how surprising the data would be under that assumption; it is not the probability the hypothesis itself is true.

### Chapter 3: Probability and Distributions
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-03-probability-and-distributions.html

This chapter matches nine named distributions to the production mechanisms that generate them, adds joint distributions, Chebyshev's inequality, and the Law of Large Numbers, then applies Bayes' theorem, the Central Limit Theorem (including an original diagram-first three-panel figure), and the birthday problem to concrete engineering questions like alert reliability, retry budgets, and identifier collisions.

- Key concepts: Bayes' theorem and the base-rate fallacy; normal/binomial/Poisson/exponential/geometric/Bernoulli/uniform/lognormal/hypergeometric distributions; joint distributions and independence; Chebyshev's inequality; the Law of Large Numbers; the 68-95-99.7 rule and z-scores; the Central Limit Theorem; the birthday problem
- Interactive figures: fig-bayes (P(true incident given alert) vs. base rate), fig-normal-rule (68-95-99.7 rule across standard deviations), fig-zscore (tail probability vs. z threshold), fig-uniform, fig-bernoulli, fig-binomial-conversions, fig-geometric (attempts until a flaky call succeeds), fig-poisson, fig-exponential, fig-lognormal (a right-skewed latency distribution), fig-chebyshev (a distribution-free bound on how much mass can sit far from the mean), fig-joint (a joint distribution over two correlated production signals), fig-lln (a running average converging to the true mean as sample size grows), fig-clt-three-panel (raw data, mean-of-8, and mean-of-32 samples, diagram-first), fig-clt (sample means becoming normal-shaped as n grows), fig-birthday (collision probability vs. identifier length)
- FAQ: If an anomaly detector is 95% sensitive, is a firing alert 95% likely to indicate a true incident? No. At a 1% base rate of true incidents, Bayes' theorem gives roughly an 8.8% chance the alert reflects a true incident, because the detector's false-alarm rate on the much larger pool of non-incident hours dominates the total number of alerts.

## Part 2: Regression and Predictive Modeling

### Chapter 4: Regression Modeling
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-04-regression-modeling.html

Covers ordinary least squares, confidence vs. prediction intervals, multiple regression with categorical/dummy encoding and interaction terms, multicollinearity diagnostics via the variance inflation factor, high-cardinality categorical binning by residual, logistic regression with classification-metrics groundwork, model-fit metrics (R-squared, adjusted R-squared, AIC, BIC), statistical vs. practical significance, and regularization (Lasso, Ridge, Elastic Net), closing with a Bayesian preview showing Ridge and Lasso as posterior modes under Gaussian and Laplace priors.

- Key concepts: ordinary least squares (OLS); confidence intervals vs. prediction intervals; multiple regression and holding other predictors constant; categorical predictors and dummy encoding; interaction terms; the variance inflation factor (VIF) and multicollinearity; high-cardinality categorical binning by residual; logistic regression and classification-metrics groundwork (accuracy, precision, recall); AIC/BIC and adjusted R-squared; Lasso (L1), Ridge (L2), and Elastic Net regularization
- Interactive figures: fig-ols, fig-ci-pi (confidence band vs. prediction band), fig-multiple-regression, fig-region-dummy-effect (a categorical predictor's dummy-encoded effect), fig-interaction-slopes (an interaction term changing the slope by group), fig-vif (multicollinearity's effect on coefficient variance), fig-endpoint-residual-binning (a high-cardinality categorical predictor binned by residual), fig-logistic, fig-confusion-threshold, fig-r2 (R-squared vs. adjusted R-squared with noise predictors), fig-aic-bic, fig-significance (a fixed effect crossing significance purely from sample size), fig-regularization (Lasso vs. Ridge coefficient paths), fig-bayesian-ridge (posterior narrowing as prior variance shrinks)
- FAQ: What is the difference between a confidence interval and a prediction interval? A confidence interval estimates the range likely to contain the true mean outcome and narrows as sample size grows; a prediction interval estimates the range for one future observation and stays wide because it also accounts for irreducible individual variability.

### Chapter 5: Cross-Validation and Model Selection
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-05-cross-validation.html

Explains why training error can't select a model, then builds up the validation-set approach, leave-one-out cross-validation, and k-fold cross-validation built entirely from scratch (a manual fold-assignment loop and hyperparameter grid search) before introducing scikit-learn's convenience wrappers, applies k-fold CV to select a regularization strength, and covers what CV cannot fix (data leakage, non-independent time-series data), ending with the Bayesian analog PSIS-LOO/ELPD.

- Key concepts: validation-set approach; leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV); k-fold cross-validation built from scratch and the bias-variance trade-off in choosing k; data leakage and non-independence; PSIS-LOO and expected log predictive density (ELPD)
- Interactive figures: fig-train-test-error (U-shaped test error vs. polynomial degree), fig-validation-variance (estimate spread across split strategies), fig-lambda-selection (cross-validated error curve for choosing Lasso's lambda), fig-knn-grid-search (a from-scratch k-fold grid search over two hyperparameters), fig-elpd-by-complexity
- FAQ: Why is k=5 or k=10 the standard choice for k-fold cross-validation? Both values keep training-fold bias low while largely avoiding the high correlation-driven variance that affects LOOCV, making them an empirically supported default.

### Chapter 6: Moving Beyond Linearity: Regression Splines
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-06-regression-splines.html

Uses a load-latency saturation curve to motivate moving past straight-line regression, covering polynomial regression's Runge-phenomenon instability, basis functions, regression splines and knot count, natural cubic splines, smoothing splines, LOESS local regression, generalized additive models (GAMs) with a partial-residual-plot device for reading one spline term's contribution, and Gaussian process regression as the Bayesian extension.

- Key concepts: polynomial regression and the Runge phenomenon; basis functions; regression splines and knot placement; natural cubic splines; smoothing splines (roughness penalty); LOESS (local regression); generalized additive models (GAMs) and partial residual plots; Gaussian process regression
- Interactive figures: fig-linear-misfit, fig-poly-degree (Runge-phenomenon wobble at the boundary), fig-basis-functions, fig-knot-count, fig-natural-boundary, fig-smoothing-lambda, fig-loess-span (LOESS fit smoothing as the span widens), fig-gam-components (a GAM's per-predictor component functions), fig-gam-partial-residual (a partial-residual plot isolating one spline term's contribution), fig-gp-posterior
- FAQ: Why does a natural cubic spline behave better than a regular cubic spline near the edge of the data? It adds the constraint that the function must be linear (not cubic) beyond the boundary knots, trading a little flexibility at the extremes for predictable extrapolation instead of letting the curve keep bending past the last knot.

### Chapter 7: Tree-Based Methods: Decision Trees and Random Forests
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-07-decision-trees-random-forests.html

Builds a canary-deployment rollback classifier to cover regression and classification trees (RSS, Gini index, entropy), cost-complexity pruning, tree instability, bagging, random forests, and a dedicated section on evaluating a classifier, precision, recall, F1, and the ROC curve, followed by a multi-model decision-boundary comparison, a three-way variable-importance comparison (permutation vs. Gini vs. entropy) that shows the methods can disagree, and Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) for per-prediction credible intervals.

- Key concepts: recursive binary splitting and RSS; Gini index and entropy; cost-complexity (weakest-link) pruning; bagging and random forests (random feature subset, out-of-bag error); precision/recall/F1/ROC-AUC; decision boundaries across model families; permutation vs. Gini vs. entropy variable importance and high-cardinality-feature bias; Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
- Interactive figures: fig-split-criteria, fig-tree-overfitting, fig-pruning-path, fig-tree-instability, fig-oob-error, fig-confusion-threshold (drag the classification threshold to live-update the confusion matrix, precision/recall/F1 bars, and ROC marker), fig-variable-importance, fig-importance-comparison (permutation vs. Gini vs. entropy importance disagreeing on a high-cardinality nuisance feature), fig-decision-boundaries (a single tree, a random forest, and logistic regression compared on the same data), fig-bart-vs-rf
- FAQ: Why does a random forest split on only a random subset of predictors at each split instead of all of them? It forces trees to occasionally split on weaker predictors instead of always defaulting to the strongest one, decorrelating the trees so averaging reduces variance more effectively.

### Chapter 8: Gradient Boosting: XGBoost and LightGBM
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-08-gradient-boosting.html

Explains gradient boosting as sequential, error-correcting tree fitting, covers shrinkage/learning rate and early stopping, a regularized-vs-unregularized overfitting curve showing validation error turning upward while training error keeps falling, XGBoost's regularized second-order boosting objective, LightGBM's histogram splitting and leaf-wise growth with GOSS, practical guidance for choosing among random forest/XGBoost/LightGBM, and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization via Gaussian processes.

- Key concepts: gradient boosting via negative-gradient fitting; shrinkage (learning rate) and early stopping; regularized vs. unregularized overfitting; XGBoost's regularized, second-order boosting objective; LightGBM's histogram-based splitting and leaf-wise growth; gradient-based one-side sampling (GOSS)
- Interactive figures: fig-boosting-rounds, fig-shrinkage-early-stopping, fig-overfitting-curve (train and validation error across boosting rounds, regularized vs. unregularized), fig-xgboost-regularization, fig-leafwise-vs-levelwise, fig-model-comparison-size (random forest vs. gradient boosting as training size grows), fig-gp-hyperparameter-search
- FAQ: Why are boosted trees kept shallow while random forest trees are grown deep? A random forest controls variance through averaging many deep trees; a boosted model keeps trees shallow on purpose so no single tree overcorrects, leaving learning rate and tree count to control ensemble complexity instead.

## Part 3: Bayesian Methods

### Chapter 9: Bayesian Linear Regression and Regularization
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-09-bayesian-regression.html

Rebuilds Chapter 4's latency regression with full Bayesian machinery: conjugate posteriors, credible vs. confidence intervals, Ridge/Lasso/horseshoe priors, robust regression with a Student-t likelihood, hierarchical (multilevel) regression letting services borrow statistical strength from each other, a step-by-step Metropolis-Hastings MCMC walkthrough, an explanation of why divergences happen (funnel geometry, non-centered parameterization), PyMC-based logistic regression, MCMC convergence diagnostics, and prior and posterior predictive checks.

- Key concepts: conjugate Gaussian posterior; credible interval vs. confidence interval; Ridge (Gaussian prior), Lasso (Laplace prior), and horseshoe prior; robust regression with a Student-t likelihood; hierarchical (multilevel) regression and partial pooling; Metropolis-Hastings MCMC mechanics; why MCMC divergences happen and non-centered parameterization; MCMC convergence diagnostics (R-hat, ess_bulk, divergent transitions); prior predictive checks; posterior predictive checks
- Interactive figures: fig-posterior-narrowing, fig-ci-repeated-experiments, fig-credible-interval-single, fig-prior-shapes, fig-shrinkage-profile, fig-robust-regression (Normal vs. Student-t likelihood on outlier-contaminated data), fig-hierarchical-regression (no-pooling, complete-pooling, and partial-pooling estimates compared across services), fig-metropolis-walkthrough (Metropolis-Hastings accept/reject mechanics step by step), fig-divergences-funnel (centered vs. non-centered parameterization and the funnel geometry), fig-bayesian-logistic, fig-rhat-diagnostic, fig-prior-predictive-check, fig-posterior-predictive-check
- FAQ: What is the difference between a 95% credible interval and a 95% confidence interval? A credible interval is a direct probability statement given the observed data; a confidence interval is a statement about a repeated procedure, with no probability claim about any single interval.

### Chapter 10: Bayesian Model Selection and Comparison
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-10-bayesian-model-selection.html

Shows that WAIC and PSIS-LOO answer the same generalization question as k-fold cross-validation but computed directly from a Bayesian model's posterior draws, using ArviZ's model-comparison tools on the latency regression, adds posterior predictive checks as a distinct model-adequacy diagnostic, Bayesian model averaging, a Bayes factors treatment with a callout on why this chapter leads with predictive-accuracy metrics instead, a worked example of WAIC and PSIS-LOO disagreeing on model ranking, and a KL-divergence grounding of the chapter's "closer to the truth" narrative.

- Key concepts: log pointwise predictive density; WAIC and effective number of parameters; PSIS-LOO; Pareto k-hat diagnostic; elpd_loo/elpd_waic comparison; posterior predictive checks as a model-adequacy diagnostic; Bayesian model averaging; Bayes factors and their prior/sample-size sensitivity; KL-divergence grounding of predictive accuracy
- Interactive figures: fig-lpd-per-point, fig-khat-diagnostic, fig-waic-ploo-complexity, fig-waic-loo-disagreement (an engineered case where WAIC and PSIS-LOO rank models differently), fig-elpd-compare, fig-ppc-check (visual posterior predictive check plus a Bayesian p-value), fig-model-averaging (a predictive blend weighted by each model's pseudo-BMA weight)
- FAQ: When should you use PSIS-LOO instead of k-fold cross-validation? When the model is Bayesian anyway, the dataset is too small for stable k-fold refitting, or the k-hat diagnostic's influential-point warning is valuable on its own; for routine comparisons, k-fold CV remains faster.

### Chapter 11: Bayesian Nonlinear Regression: Gaussian Processes
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-11-bayesian-gaussian-processes.html

Replaces Chapter 6's smoothing spline with a Gaussian process that returns a full posterior distribution over curves, covering kernel choice, closed-form conditioning, length-scale selection via marginal likelihood, automatic relevance determination, a periodic-kernel composition for signals that repeat, a full Bayesian (MCMC) treatment of GP hyperparameters, Gaussian process classification via a sigmoid-linked latent function, and honest extrapolation.

- Key concepts: GP prior over functions and length-scale; RBF and Matern kernels; closed-form posterior via multivariate-normal conditioning; marginal likelihood maximization; automatic relevance determination (ARD); periodic kernels and kernel composition; full Bayesian (MCMC) treatment of GP hyperparameters; Gaussian process classification (latent function, sigmoid link, Bernoulli likelihood)
- Interactive figures: fig-prior-samples, fig-kernel-comparison, fig-posterior-fit, fig-extrapolation, fig-length-scale-fit, fig-ard-length-scales, fig-periodic-kernel (composing a periodic kernel to capture a daily cycle), fig-full-bayes-hyperparams (a point-estimate fit vs. a fully sampled length-scale posterior), fig-gp-classification-boundary (a GP classifier tracking a non-monotonic boundary that logistic regression misses)
- FAQ: Why does a Gaussian process's credible band widen sharply past the observed data range? The kernel's correlation with training data decays with distance, so past the last observation the posterior reverts toward the wide prior, signaling that the model has run out of evidence rather than malfunctioning.

### Chapter 12: Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART)
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-12-bayesian-bart.html

Builds BART as a sum-of-weak-trees model fit by MCMC (Bayesian backfitting) that returns a full posterior over a rollback-risk score, applied to the Chapter 7 canary rollback classifier, with an explanation of the sigmoid link BART needs for classification and what a divergence (or its absence) means for BART's particle-Gibbs sampler.

- Key concepts: sum-of-weak-trees ensemble vs. random forest averaging; tree-structure, leaf-value, and error-variance priors; Bayesian backfitting; the sigmoid link for BART classification; particle-Gibbs (PGBART) sampling and what a divergence count means for it; posterior-based variable importance
- Interactive figures: fig-ensemble-buildup, fig-tree-structure-prior, fig-leaf-value-prior, fig-mcmc-trace, fig-bart-vs-rf-interval, fig-bart-variable-importance
- FAQ: How does BART's variable importance differ from a random forest's? BART counts split frequency across every tree and posterior draw, producing a distribution that shows draw-to-draw uncertainty; a random forest's Gini-based importance gives a single bar per feature with no uncertainty.

### Chapter 13: Bayesian Approaches to Gradient Boosting
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-13-bayesian-boosting.html

Explains why gradient boosting has no clean posterior, then covers the practical Bayesian-adjacent workarounds: Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, NGBoost's distributional predictions (and where a single-distribution-family output breaks under multimodal residuals), quantile regression for predicting a specific quantile like the SLA-relevant P95 instead of the mean, and conformal prediction for a distribution-free coverage guarantee.

- Key concepts: why boosting lacks a posterior; Bayesian hyperparameter optimization via Gaussian process/TPE surrogate models; NGBoost predicting distribution parameters via a proper scoring rule, and its limits under multimodal residuals; quantile regression for tail-relevant predictions; conformal prediction and distribution-free coverage guarantees
- Interactive figures: fig-bo-search-trajectory, fig-expected-improvement, fig-ngboost-width, fig-quantile-regression (predicting the P95 instead of the mean, sliding across quantiles), fig-conformal-coverage (naive vs. conformalized coverage across load segments)
- FAQ: If a project needs a full Bayesian posterior over a boosting-like ensemble, what should be used instead? BART (Chapter 12), since it delivers an additive-tree ensemble with a full posterior and comparable tabular-data performance, while Bayesian hyperparameter optimization and NGBoost only solve narrower problems.

### Chapter 14: Bayesian Experimentation for A/B Testing
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-14-bayesian-ab-testing.html

Presents Bayesian A/B testing as a full alternative to frequentist hypothesis testing, covering Beta-Binomial conjugacy, win probability, expected loss as a stopping rule, the peeking problem, and Normal-Normal conjugacy for continuous metrics, then adds sample-ratio-mismatch (SRM) checks, multiple-metric correction, a hierarchical A/B testing example with partial pooling across observed segments, and a latent (unobserved) subgroup mixture-model example, on a checkout-button redesign experiment.

- Key concepts: Beta-Binomial conjugacy; win probability; expected loss as a stopping rule; the peeking/optional-stopping problem; Normal-Normal conjugacy for continuous metrics; sample ratio mismatch (SRM) checks; the multiple-metric correction problem; hierarchical A/B testing across observed segments; latent (unobserved) subgroup heterogeneity via a mixture model
- Interactive figures: fig-ab-prior-shapes, fig-posterior-update, fig-ab-overlay, fig-decision-metrics, fig-ab-peeking, fig-normal-normal-update, fig-srm-check (a traffic-split chi-square check catching a redirect bug), fig-multiple-metrics (false-positive inflation across many tracked metrics, corrected vs. uncorrected), fig-hierarchical-segments (partial pooling across observed traffic-source segments), fig-latent-mixture (a two-component mixture surfacing an unlogged subgroup)
- FAQ: Does Bayesian A/B testing solve the peeking problem? Not entirely. A Bayesian posterior doesn't inflate mechanically the way a repeated significance test does, but optional stopping still produces a noisier, biased estimate than a sample size decided in advance.

### Chapter 15: Conclusion
URL: https://rudrendupaul.github.io/python-statistics-for-data-science-ml-ai-engineers/chapters/chapter-15-conclusion.html

Closes the book by tracing the running checkout-API dataset across all fourteen prior chapters, naming recurring throughlines (including a callback to the confusion-matrix/ROC-AUC additions in Chapters 7 and 8), and framing Part 2 and Part 3 as two complementary lenses on the same questions rather than competing camps.

- Key concepts: summary statistics hiding structure; confounding as a design-level problem no model can repair; frequentist point estimates vs. Bayesian posteriors as paired lenses (Ch4/Ch9, Ch5/Ch10, Ch6/Ch11, Ch7/Ch12, Ch8/Ch13, Ch2/Ch14); a number is not an answer until it survives a check, extended to classification metrics; explicit scope boundary (no multi-armed bandits, causal inference for observational data, or deep learning)
- FAQ: Does a Bayesian posterior fix a poorly designed or confounded experiment? No. Bayesian methods change how uncertainty is quantified but do not repair a comparison that was never fair to begin with; a Bayesian posterior is just as vulnerable to a confounder as a frequentist p-value is.
